title: MA9-12687
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: Mrs. XXXX XXXX, citizen of Burundi, asks for asylum under sections 96 and 97 (1) b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The Minister of Public Safety intervenes and asks that the claimant be excluded from the benefit of the protection of Canada, following section 98 of the IRPA and section 1 F a) of the United Convention on Refugee Status.

The claimant was met by a Tribunal officer who had recommended, in a detailed report, that she be recognized as "Convention Refugee" without a hearing1, according to section 19 of the RPD rules. However, in accordance with section 19(5) of the Rules, the Tribunal sent the case for a full hearing2, given the claimant's functions with the Burundian government, and asked for the Minister's intervention in her case.
The claimants' identity was established to the satisfaction of the Tribunal, by satisfactory identity documents3.

The claimant is a Burundian citizen of Tutsi ethnicity. She, like all Burundians, suffered from the war in her country that started in 1993. Her husband, XXXX XXXX, was assassinated on XXXX XXXX, 1994 because he was on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant was then XXXX at the Ministry of XXXX; few months later, she was appointed as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX in XXXX 19XXXX, then in Russia in 19XXXX, then finally in XXXX from 20XXXX to 20XXXX, after a return to Burundi where she was XXXX, then XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

Since her appointment in her post in XXXX, she started to be the victim of intimidation, harassment, because of her involvement with human rights and women organizations, and because of her Tutsi ethnicity, as she related in great details in her narrative4, and at the end she was even receiving threats. In XXXX 2009, she was recalled to Burundi and deprived of her functions as an XXXX. Fearing for her life, she asked for asylum on XXXX XXXX, 2009.
The claimant also fears for her life in relation to her never successful attempts to receive financial compensation from the insurance companies after her husband's death.

The Minister alleges that the claimant, having been a XXXX XXXX of the Burundian government in various functions inside and outside her country for numerous years, including eight years as XXXX in the period from 19XXXX to 20XXXX, has been complicit in crimes against humanity perpetrated and/or sanctioned by the Burundian government against the Burundian Hutu population during her years as a XXXX XXXX of that government. Consequently, the Minister asks that she be excluded from the benefit of the protection of Canada, in accordance with section 98 of the IRPA. Documentary evidence

The Minister's evidence is voluminous and damning : the Burundian armed and security forces committed, from 19XXXX to 20XXXX, serious human rights violations such as rape of women and girls5, forced displacement of civilian populations for example 350 000 civilians camps surrounding Bujumbura in 20006 and 30 000 civilians in Ruyigi at the spring of 20027, massacres and extrajudicial executions of civilians8, torture9.
This evidence is not contested by the claimant. I am of the opinion, for the following reasons, that these acts described in the documentary evidence constitute crimes against humanity.

The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court states at section 7(1) that murder, forcible transfer, imprisonment or other sever deprivation of physical liberty in violation of fundamental rules of international law, rape and other forms of serious sexual violence, persecution, enforced disappearance and other inhuman acts of a similar nature, when committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population constitute crimes against humanity.

Lately, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled in Mugesera10: "As we shall see, based on the provisions of the Criminal Code and the principles of international law, a criminal act rises to the level of a crime against humanity when four elements are made out: 1. An enumerated proscribed act was committed (this involves showing that the accused committed the criminal act and had the requisite guilty state of mind for the underlying act); 2. The act was committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack; 3. The attack was directed against any civilian population or any identifiable group of persons; and 4. The person committing the proscribed act knew of the attack and knew or took the risk that his or her act comprised a part of that attack."

I am of the opinion that the acts described in the documentary evidence, committed from 19XXXX to 20XXXX, are crimes against humanity as they meet all the above mentioned criteria: they were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population, following a plan.

The determinative question is therefore the following: did the claimant participate in the said acts? It is not alleged that the claimant ever herself committed any of the acts mentioned and characterized above; however, she may have participated as an accomplice. Complicity

Jurisprudence indicates that complicity implies a common purpose, a personal and knowing participation to the acts committed by that organisation. More particularly, if someone who is associated with such an organisation does not take measures to stop the acts he is aware are occurring, if he can, nor disassociates himself from the organisation at the earliest possible time, but to the contrary actively participate in the organisation, demonstrates a shared common purpose. Therefore mens rea is an important aspect of complicity. As stated in Thomas11 : "The law makes it clear that in order to be complicit in the commission of an international offence, an individual's participation must be personal and knowing. Complicity in such an offence rests on a shared common purpose: Gutierrez, above at para. 22, citing Penate, above at para. 4 This has been described as the mens rea requirement of the exclusion clause: Cardenas v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] F.C.J. No. 139 at para. 12 (T.D.) (QL) [Cardenas]."

Moreover, jurisprudence has established that complicity may be drawn if an individual is a member of an organization which commits crimes against humanity, if that person knowingly participated in or tolerated them12.

And this applies even if the person did not know in advance the crimes that were going to be committed, but only learned it as they were occurring, if the person then does not act to dissociate herself from the crimes. As stated by Justice Tremblay-Lamer : " La preuve ne démontre pas non plus que le demandeur avait connaissance des crimes à mesure qu'ils étaient commis, en contraste, par exemple, avec l'affaire Sivakumar, précitée. Néanmoins, il n'est pas déterminant que l'intéressé sache de manière générale que de tels crimes de guerre et crimes contre l'humanité ont été commis ; il doit plutôt manifester une intention commune, ne serait-ce que par sa propre inaction, avec ceux qui les commettent : arrêt Ramirez, précité. "13

In Bukumba14, the Federal Court stated the following : "An individual may be an accomplice to an international crime if, having knowledge of that crime, he fails to take steps to prevent it occurring or to disengage himself from the offending organization at the earliest possibility consistent with his own safety (Penate v. Canada, [1994] 2 FC 79)"

But the ruling that most resembles the claimant's situation is the Federal Court of Appeal recent decision in Ezokola, which also dealt with a senior diplomat in an embassy of a government whose army and security forces had committed crimes against humanity. In that case, the claimant was a XXXX for XXXX years; in the present case the claimant was herself the XXXX for XXXX years in a XXXX years period. Justice Noël ruled to the following15: "A senior official may, by remaining in his of her position without protest and continuing to defend the interests of his or her government while being aware of the crimes committed by this government demonstrate "personal and knowing participation" in these crimes and be complicit with the government in their commission."

The criteria to determine whether the claimant is an accomplice of acts committed by her government, I will use the following six criteria in order to determine complicity: " 1- the nature of the organization; 2- the method of recruitment; 3- position/rank in the organization; 4- knowledge of the organization's atrocities; 5- the length of time in the organization; and 6- the opportunity to leave the organization. "16 (1) Nature of the organization
As admitted by both parties, the Burundian government has a legitimate purpose and is not an organization directed to a brutal limited purpose. (2) Method of recruitment

The claimant testified that when she was appointed as XXXX in early 19XXXX, she was already serving her country as XXXX for the Ministry of XXXX, since XXXX 19XXXX17. Although it came as a surprise as she testified - she learned of her appointment XXXX XXXX XXXX -, the claimant welcomed it as she needed to increase her salary; she was the only support for her children, after the brutal death of her husband few months before. Therefore I conclude that the claimant joined her position voluntarily. (3) Position/rank in the organization

When the claimant was appointed XXXX, she was already in position of responsibility in the Ministry of XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. And with her appointment as an XXXX, she obtained the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. And when she returned to Burundi in 20XXXX XXXX between her second and third post, she also had a very important position in the government, serving as a XXXX then promptly as the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for XXXX years. (4) Knowledge of the organization's atrocities

The claimant acknowledged that she always knew the atrocities that were being committed by the armed and security forces in her country. More particularly, during her post as XXXX in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, she had many opportunities to read reports from abuses committed in Burundi and even to discuss the situation with representatives of human rights and development organizations. She testified that she was never given instructions to hide the information she knew about the conditions in her country. (5) Length of time in the organization
The claimant was XXXX for a total of XXXX years in a XXXX years period. I consider that this is a lengthy period of time. (6) Opportunity to leave the organization or to disengage from the abuses

This is where the claimant vehemently defended her point of view against the Minister. The Minister argues that the claimant remained in her position of XXXX, representing her government abroad even if she knew clearly that the government she had a duty to represent was committing crimes against humanity for all the period of her employment, and from before that period.

The claimant was asked whether she could have resigned her position, in order to disassociate herself from this abusive government; she answered that she could have, but as a widow and a single mother, she needed to have sufficient financial means to provide for her children, and given that the government is practically the only employer in Burundi, she would have had difficulties to find employment. I do not accept this argument for the following reasons. I understand that the claimant wanted to have sufficient financial means to assure a good future for her XXXX. However, the extent of the atrocities committed by the government she had to represent and support - this being the essence of her work as XXXX, is such that the fact of representing that government sends the message of a silent acquiescence of the atrocities committed. And when she was informed, by other diplomats as she testified, of the ongoing atrocities, she should have resigned, in the name of humanity; her economic argument is not reasonable given the extent of the abuses.

I note that the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Burundi resigned in 1996, accusing the government of failing to protect its citizens18. The claimant chose to remain in post and never resigned; her post as XXXX ended when she was recalled by the government.

The claimant argues that she consistently sought help from other XXXX to try to find a solution to the ongoing abuses that were occurring in Burundi. In a written statement produced in the present file19, she declared that she repeatedly expressed her disagreement with the crimes committed in her country, as she writes: "through contacts that I had with people who could influence the course of things in one way or another", for example the XXXX and XXXX XXXX. She added that sometimes it is they who informed her of the situation. Also while back in Burundi as a XXXX of XXXX XXXX, she spoke to high officials of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. But the situation in her country did not improve; yet she remained in her position. I am of the opinion that then she should have expressed her views in a more direct way by resigning, even at the cost of financial hardship.

I have evaluated the whole evidence, I have considered the claimant's testimony, especially in that regard, however I find that her long term service at such an important position, benefiting of a high standard of life, is compelling evidence of not only a silent acquiescence to the atrocities committed by her government, but of an active support of that government.

For all the above mentioned reasons, I conclude that there are serious reasons for considering that the provisions of Section 1F a) of the Convention apply to the claimant XXXX XXXX, in that there are serious reasons to believe that she participated by complicity, in crimes against humanity.

Consequently XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection", as stipulated in section 98 of the IRPA.
